issues.legal_issue: A deceased tenant’s commercial tenancy remains heritable after termination of the contractual tenancy, and the heirs inherit the protection against eviction where the governing rent law imposes no restriction on succession to commercial tenancies.
material_facts: The deceased tenant occupied commercial premises and his contractual tenancy had been terminated.
He continued in possession under the protection of the rent-control law when he died during the eviction proceedings.

The governing law treated a person continuing in possession after termination as a tenant and provided no restriction on inheritance of commercial tenancy rights, although it restricted succession to residential tenancies.
The High Court ordered eviction on the ground that the heirs of a tenant whose contractual tenancy had ended did not inherit the tenancy or its statutory protection.
issues.conclusion: The tenancy rights in the commercial premises devolved on the deceased tenant’s heirs under the ordinary law of succession, and the heirs inherited the Act’s protection against eviction. The High Court’s order was set aside and the case remanded for the appeal and cross-objection to be decided on their merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(1)(ii) and 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a person continuing in possession after termination of the contractual tenancy remains a tenant protected against eviction except on grounds specified by the Act. The Act does not, merely by terminating the contractual tenancy, extinguish the tenant’s estate or interest; that interest is heritable unless the Act provides otherwise. Section 2(1)(iii), introduced by the Delhi Rent Control (Amendment) Act, 1976, restricts succession in respect of residential premises but does not restrict inheritance of commercial tenancy rights. In the absence of such a restriction, those rights pass under the ordinary law of succession. The Court followed Damadilal v. Parashram and relied on V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal; it held that contrary observations in Ganpat Ladha v. Sashikant Vishnu Shinde did not state the correct law.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and contractual_tenancy_terminated and tenant_remained_in_possession and premises_are_commercial and governing_law_recognizes_continued_possession_as_tenancy and no_inheritance_restriction_for_commercial_premises

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The dispute arose in a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.contractual_tenancy_terminated: The landlord had ended the tenant’s contractual tenancy.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_possession: The tenant continued to occupy the premises after the contractual tenancy ended and before an eviction order was made.
predicates.premises_are_commercial: The premises were occupied for commercial use.
predicates.governing_law_recognizes_continued_posse: The governing law treated a person remaining in possession after termination of the tenancy as a tenant.
predicates.no_inheritance_restriction_for_commercia: The governing law did not restrict inheritance of tenancy rights in commercial premises.

issues.definition: When an eviction dispute concerns commercial premises and the tenant remained in possession after contractual termination under a law that recognizes that continued possession as tenancy but does not restrict commercial succession, the heirs inherit the tenancy rights and rent-control protection.
